subChunks.title: JUnit 5: Writing & Organising Tests

storyBeats.text: Eldrin ceremonially adds a new spell to the Academy Grimoire. But first, he runs the verification ritual — every test case must pass or the spell is rejected.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A test is a spell contract. It declares: given this input, I expect this output. Run the tests; if they pass, the contract holds. Change the code; run the tests again. Any broken contract is found immediately, not three months later in production.

storyBeats.label: Test pattern

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Good test names read like specifications: adding two positive numbers returns their sum. @DisplayName lets you write natural language test names. The test suite becomes living documentation of your code's behaviour.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a StringUtils class with method isPalindrome(String s) that returns true if the string reads the same forwards and backwards. Demonstrate the logic with assertions (manual, not JUnit).
guidedPractice.hint: Use new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString() and compare with equals().

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the role of @BeforeEach in JUnit 5. Why is it important to create a fresh instance before each test?

options: That the lambda throws the specified exception type
That the lambda does not throw any exception
That the lambda runs in under 1 second
questions.answer: That the lambda throws the specified exception type
questions.explanation: assertThrows passes if and only if the lambda throws the specified exception type. It fails if no exception is thrown or a different exception type is thrown.

subChunks.title: Mockito & TDD

storyBeats.text: Eldrin needs to test the Academy's enrollment service — but the actual database is across the country. He conjures a mock registry that behaves exactly as instructed.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A mock is a puppet — it responds exactly as you script it, without having any actual behaviour of its own. You test how your code interacts with the mock, not how the real dependency works. Your unit tests become fast, isolated, and reliable.

storyBeats.label: Mock pattern

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: TDD inverts the usual sequence. You write the test first — describing what the code should do. The test fails immediately (red). Then you write the code to make it pass (green). Then you clean up (refactor). The tests guard against regressions forever.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a manual TDD cycle: write an interface SpellRepo with findSpell(String name), a mock implementation, a SpellService that uses it, and demonstrate it returns the correct spell name.
guidedPractice.hint: MockSpellRepo checks if name equals "Fireball" and returns different strings accordingly.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is Mockito used for in testing? Explain the red-green-refactor TDD cycle.

questions.prompt: In TDD, what is the correct order of the cycle?
options: Write failing test → make it pass → refactor
Write test → refactor → make it pass
questions.answer: Write failing test → make it pass → refactor
questions.explanation: Red (failing test) → Green (minimal code to pass) → Refactor (clean up). The failing test first ensures you have a real requirement and that your test actually tests something.

subChunks.title: BDD & Integration Testing

storyBeats.text: Eldrin presents the test pyramid etched on the academy wall — a wide base of unit tests, a narrower middle of integration tests, a tiny tip of end-to-end tests.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: BDD bridges the gap between the business and the developer. When a test reads like 'Given an enrolled apprentice, When they complete a chapter, Then their XP increases by 100' — even the Academy Headmaster can verify the system behaves correctly.

storyBeats.label: BDD structure

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The test pyramid is economics. Unit tests are cheap — fast to write, fast to run, easy to debug. Integration tests are expensive. End-to-end tests are very expensive. Maximise unit tests; use integration tests for critical paths; use E2E tests sparingly.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a Wizard class with mana management. Using Given-When-Then style (comments), test: casting a spell that costs 40 mana from 100 (succeeds, mana = 60) and casting when mana is insufficient (fails, mana unchanged).
guidedPractice.hint: castSpell(cost) returns false and leaves mana unchanged when cost > mana.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the test pyramid. How do unit, integration, and end-to-end tests differ, and why should unit tests outnumber the others?

questions.prompt: What is the 'Given-When-Then' structure in BDD tests?
options: Setup preconditions / trigger action / verify outcome
questions.answer: Setup preconditions / trigger action / verify outcome
questions.explanation: Given = arrange the test preconditions; When = act (trigger the behaviour under test); Then = assert (verify the outcome). This structure produces readable, requirement-like tests.
